abstract: Selective attention requires target identification and exclusion of irrelevant information. We distinguished substitution and concomitant distractor intrusions in 29 adults performing rapid serial visual presentation with uncertain target number. Substitution reports, in which only the distractor was reported, showed an attenuated and delayed N2 posterior contralateral (N2pc) component and a smaller P3b; intrusion probability decreased with target-distractor numerical distance. Concomitant reports included both identities without reliable differences in measured averaged event-related potentials from correct reports of the same sequence. However, target-first concomitant reports were distinguishable through distributed activity and showed reduced left-frontal power, predominantly in theta. Comparisons with correct single- and dual-target reports indicated that reporting two identities did not simply reproduce genuine two-target processing. These findings distinguish processing profiles of substitution and concomitant intrusions and extend temporal-selection accounts from attentional engagement to subsequent regulation of which processed identities enter report.
